newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir violence rages on despite local rule.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir violence rages on despite local rule.

text.p: Three months after the restoration of local rule in Kashmir, violence continues unabated in the Himalayan region, police and residents said on Wednesday.
There has been no let-up in the killings which have punctuated the seven-year-old rebellion, they said.
The continued violence has cast doubt on the new state government's ability to quell the revolt, which has its roots in a 50-year-old quarrel between Pakistan and India.
State assembly elections last September -- the first local polls since a separatist revolt erupted in 1990 -- had raised hopes militancy could be defused.
Chief Minister Farooq Abdullah wasted little time in October offering to hold talks with unarmed separatists. Just as quickly, they turned him down.

"Unexpectedly, Farooq's government has brought no perceptible change in the situation after seven years," Noor Ahmad Baba, head of the political science department at the University of Kashmir, told Reuters.
"If the present rate of violence continues, there are bad days ahead for this government."
According to police, there were 40 bomb explosions and 55 grenade attacks in November and December, up from 35 explosions and 38 attacks in July and August.
Last Friday a powerful bomb planted in a scooter taxi exploded near Abdullah's official residence, killing seven people, police said. Abdullah was out of the country.
Jamait-ul-Mujahideen, a militant group fighting for Kashmir to join neighbouring Pakistan, claimed responsibility for the blast, which came two days after a grenade attack on a state junior minister.
A total of 325 people were killed in insurgency-related incidents in the Kashmir valley over the past two months, down from some 400 in July and August, police said.
But they said cold winter weather usually leads to a sharp decline in violence.
Security officials said hundreds of militants, many of whom have crossed illegally into Kashmir, were hiding out in remote forests, waiting for warmer weather.
"The infiltration across the border by militants has been on the increase ever since elections were held," said a senior police officer in Srinagar, the state's summer capital.
India accuses Pakistan, which rules one-third of Kashmir and has staked a claim to the rest, of arming and training militants. Islamabad denies the accusation.
The state government said the spurt in bomb explosions and grenade attacks reflected the guerrillas' frustrations.

"There are remarkable achievements by the government on the developmental and political fronts. That is why militants are unnerved and resorting to criminal acts like killing of civilians," state government spokesman K.B. Jandial said.

Following a surge in violence after the polls, Abdullah named two Indian army commanders as security advisers to the state government. Authorities said the army could now carry out counter-insurgency operations without first seeking the approval of the state home (interior) ministry.
"The appointment of army advisers reflects that the ground situation has worsened," said Muzzafar Bhat, a lawyer in Kashmir's High Court.
"The holding of elections does not mean an end to militancy," Abdullah said recently. "It will not die suddenly. It takes its own time."
